prompt: In many growing cities, most new homes are now built as flats in high-rise tower blocks rather than as individual houses with gardens. Do the advantages of this trend outweigh the disadvantages?
essay:
Arguments about high-rise housing are usually arguments about particular buildings. Critics picture the neglected estates of the last century; defenders picture the well-run towers of this one. Since both describe the same building type, height alone explains very little. What separates a tower that works from one that fails is decided at street level and in the maintenance budget, and wherever both are taken seriously, the advantages of building upwards clearly outweigh the drawbacks.

The benefits of density are structural and hard to obtain otherwise. A city that expands outwards swallows farmland, lengthens every journey and spreads its population too thinly for buses, schools or local shops to pay their way. Concentrating households on one site reverses each of these at once: the bus runs frequently because enough people use it, the corner shop survives because enough people pass it, and every metre of pipe and cable serves many homes rather than a few. None of this depends on residents liking tall buildings. It follows from the arithmetic of land.

The familiar objections — isolation, crime, nowhere for children to play — are serious, but they attach to a way of building rather than to height. A tower set back from the street behind car parks and blank walls gives nobody a reason to linger at its foot, so neighbours never meet and nobody watches the entrance. Put shops, a nursery and a courtyard at its base and the same tower acquires a public life. The second failure is slower. Lifts, fire doors and heating plant shared by hundreds of households need funding for decades, and a block whose owners cannot or will not provide it becomes dangerous rather than merely shabby. A householder can mend a leaking roof; the residents of a twentieth floor cannot mend a broken lift.

The trend is therefore a good one provided cities regulate the two things developers are most tempted to neglect. Towers approved without an active ground floor, or without a maintenance fund secured before the first tenant arrives, reproduce the old estates under a new name. Built with both, they house more people, more cheaply and closer to their work than any alternative a growing city has.
title: High-rise flats instead of family houses
